planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, deeply acidic, humus-rich woodland soil in partial shade; mulch with pine bark or leaf litter and avoid disturbing roots once established.

directions: Chattooga is a named selection of flame azalea prized for its unusual soft pink petals centered with a bright golden-yellow blotch, a striking departure from the orange and red tones typical of the species. Flowers open in late spring on bare or just-leafing stems, drawing hummingbirds and swallowtail butterflies to the mountain woodland edges of the Southern Appalachians where the species is native. Like other flame azalea selections it grows into an upright, multi-stemmed shrub with fiery orange-red fall foliage that rivals the spring bloom for garden interest. Site at a woodland margin with morning sun and afternoon shade in consistently moist, acidic soil for best flowering.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, deeply acidic, humus-rich woodland soil in partial shade; does not transplant well once mature, so choose the site carefully.

directions: Cherokee is a flame azalea selection with light apricot petals set off by long, vividly red stamens, giving the flower clusters a warm two-tone glow along Appalachian ridgelines and cove forests where the wild species grows. Bloom arrives in late spring, timed with or just after leaf-out, and the wide-flared trumpets are a magnet for hummingbirds and tiger swallowtails working the woodland edge. Like the species, it colors brilliant orange-red in autumn, extending its ornamental season well past the spring floral display. Grow in moist, humus-rich, acidic soil with dappled shade from high overhead trees for the healthiest flowering.

common_name: Smokey Mountaineer Flame Azalea (Compact Reddish-Orange Selection)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, deeply acidic, humus-rich woodland soil in partial shade; its tighter, more upright habit suits smaller borders than seed-grown flame azaleas.

directions: Smokey Mountaineer was selected for brilliant reddish-orange flowers and a noticeably tighter, more upright growth habit than typical wild-collected flame azalea, making it easier to place in a designed shrub border while still reading as a true Southern Appalachian native. The two-inch trumpets open in late spring and are heavily visited by hummingbirds and swallowtail butterflies, and the compact form still delivers the species' signature glowing red fall foliage. Native flame azalea populations occur as understory shrubs on wooded mountain slopes from Georgia to Pennsylvania, and this selection retains that same tolerance for dappled woodland light. Plant in moist, acidic, well-drained soil and mulch to keep roots cool.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist, deeply acidic, humus-rich woodland soil in partial shade; site permanently, as established plants resent transplanting.

directions: Wahsega, named for the north Georgia community near Dahlonega at the edge of flame azalea's native range, is grown for flowers of an unusually deep, dark red that stand apart from the species' more common orange and yellow forms. The two-inch blooms open in late spring against bright green new foliage and pull in hummingbirds and swallowtails the way the whole species does across its Appalachian woodland range. Foliage turns a rich red-orange in autumn, giving the shrub a second season of color that echoes the spring display. Grow it as an understory shrub in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil with morning sun and afternoon shade for the most saturated flower color.

common_name: Lemon Drop Swamp Azalea (Fragrant Pastel-Yellow Selection)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in consistently moist to wet, acidic soil in partial shade; do not let roots dry out during establishment, and keep the crown at or above grade.

directions: Lemon Drop is a swamp azalea selection whose peach-tinted buds unfurl into abundant small, tubular flowers of pastel lemon-yellow, a rare warm-toned break from the white and pink flowers typical of the species. Bloom arrives in late June into July, well after most native deciduous azaleas have finished, and the flowers carry the same intense sweet, clove-like fragrance that makes swamp azalea the most fragrant of the group. In the wild the species colonizes swamps, bogs, and wet woodland margins from Maine to the Gulf Coast, and this selection keeps that preference for consistently damp, acidic soil while staying more compact than seed-grown plants. Deep red-orange fall foliage and the late, heavily perfumed bloom make it a strong choice for extending the native azalea season into summer.

common_name: Delaware Blue Swamp Azalea (Blue-Green Foliage Selection)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in consistently moist, deeply acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; keep the shallow, surface-rooted crown mulched and never let it dry out.

directions: Delaware Blue, a selection of the coastal-plain variety glaucum introduced by plantswoman Polly Hill, is grown as much for its cool, blue-green glaucous foliage as for its flowers. Clusters of shell-pink and white blooms open in late spring with sporadic repeat flowering into summer, carrying the clove-scented fragrance typical of swamp azalea, and the foliage turns a clear yellow before dropping in fall. It forms an airy, loosely branched, upright shrub well suited to a woodland border or the edge of a wet meadow, reflecting the species' native habitat in swamps and stream margins from Maine to Florida. Grow in moist to wet, acidic, organically rich soil, and note this glaucum form tolerates more open sun than typical swamp azalea if soil moisture is reliable.

common_name: Pink and Sweet Swamp Azalea (Blush Fragrant Late-Bloom Selection)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in moist to wet, deeply acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; plant shallow and mulch well, since roots are surface-feeding.

directions: Pink and Sweet is a Weston Nurseries introduction of swamp azalea selected for funnel-shaped white flowers heavily suffused with pink and carrying an especially spicy-sweet fragrance. It is among the latest-blooming native deciduous azaleas, opening well after leaf-out in early to midsummer with sporadic repeat flowers continuing into the season, which lets it fill a gap after the spring-blooming Piedmont and flame azaleas have finished. Like the species, it is native to swamps, bogs, and stream banks from the Northeast to the Gulf Coast and tolerates wetter, boggier soil than almost any other rhododendron. Grow in consistently moist, humus-rich, acidic soil, where its late, richly scented flowers will draw swallowtails and other summer pollinators.

common_name: Pink Mist Swamp Azalea (Blush White Late-Summer Selection)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in consistently moist to wet, acidic soil in partial shade; avoid letting the root zone dry out through summer.

directions: Pink Mist is a swamp azalea selection whose fragrant white flowers carry a soft haze of pink through the petal lobes, giving clusters a misted, two-tone look rather than the pure white of the wild type. It blooms notably late for a native deciduous azalea, opening in late June and continuing into July, well after the leaves have fully expanded, which extends fragrant azalea bloom into the heat of summer when few other rhododendrons are flowering. In the wild, swamp azalea grows in bogs, swamps, and stream edges from the Northeast down through the Gulf Coast, and this selection keeps that preference for reliably damp, acidic ground. Site in partial shade with consistently moist, humus-rich soil, where the clove-scented flowers will draw swallowtails and other pollinators active in midsummer.
